quiz.title: Chapter 6 Quiz: Statutes
quiz.intro: Ten questions on finding a statute, reading it in context, and using the annotated code as the research hub.

items.q: Session laws and codes differ how?
options: Session laws are by subject; codes are chronological
Session laws are published chronologically as enacted; codes reorganize them by subject
Codes are unofficial; session laws are official
items.why: The Statutes at Large are session laws; the United States Code is the code (Session Laws vs. Codes).

items.q: Why does the chapter say statutory research happens in the annotated code rather than the bare text?
options: Because the bare text is copyrighted
Because the annotated code stacks the cases construing the provision, cross-references, amendment history, secondary sources, and citator links under the text
Because the bare text is never current
items.why: One page holds the law and every pathway out of it (Answering Questions with Statutes).

items.q: You know a law is called the “Americans with Disabilities Act” but not where it is codified. The fastest finding aid is:
items.why: The Popular Name Table locates statutes by their common names (Searching for Statutes).

items.q: Reading a statute to answer a focusing question means reading:
options: The operative provision plus the definitions section, the exceptions, and the cross-referenced sections
items.why: Reading a subsection in isolation is the most damaging statutory error (Statutes and the Research Cycle; Common Pitfalls).

items.q: A statute uses the word “employer” without defining it in the section you are reading. The chapter says this:
options: Is your next question: how does this statute define employer? (then case law, legislative history, or agency interpretation)
Means the statute does not apply
Should be answered from a dictionary
items.why: Every undefined term, vague standard, exception, and cross-reference is a potential next cycle (Statutes and the Research Cycle).

items.q: When does a statute answer an application question by itself?
options: When it draws a bright line (a numeric threshold, an enumerated list, a deeming provision) and your facts map onto it without inference
Whenever it has a definitions section
Whenever a court has cited it
items.why: A limitations period is precise, but whether the clock started is usually a case-law question (Statutes and the Research Cycle).

items.q: Expressio unius is the canon that says:
options: Unambiguous text is applied as written
When a statute lists some things, it probably meant to exclude the ones it left out
Criminal statutes are read for the defendant
items.why: Treat the canons as generators of next questions; Appendix C carries the working list (Canons of Statutory Construction).

items.q: The “citing the wrong version” pitfall refers to:
options: Citing the session law instead of the code
Citing today’s text when the language in force at the time of your client’s events was different
items.why: Statutes are amended; the historical notes keep you honest (Common Pitfalls).

items.q: The annotated code’s “Implementing Regulations” note is your pathway to:
items.why: The full picture usually emerges only when you read the statute alongside its implementing regulations (Relationship Between Statutes and Regulations).

items.q: Before you can argue that legislative history resolves an ambiguity, you must first:
options: Show that the text is genuinely ambiguous
items.why: A court committed to plain meaning will never reach the legislative history (Ambiguous Statutes and Legislative History).
